Problem statement

How big the problem is

  • Hazmat transportation incidents reported to the federal hazmat safety agency, all modes, 2023: 24,265
  • Rail accidents releasing hazmat, 2016-2025: 146 (14.6 a year)
  • Their reported damage: $209.5 million ($20.9 million a year)

Sources: docs/incidents/problem_scale.tsv, docs/incidents/problem_us_damage.svg, docs/incidents/problem_scale.md

Problem statement

Already required to plan

  • Facilities filing a worst-case release scenario (title 40 Code of Federal Regulations, section 68.25): about 11,740
  • Local emergency planning committees plan for releases (Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act, section 303).
  • Built: a what-if brief from a stated wind.
  • Next: a worst-case scenario builder.
  • The author also proposes: exercises, pre-incident plans, siting, zoning.

Problem statement

Today's tools draw the area, not who is inside it

  • From 2016 to 2025, 146 rail incidents released hazmat in the contiguous United States; 4 of them in the Mid-Atlantic region our test scenarios cover.
  • Today's tools draw the area at risk; they do not say who is inside it: residents, workers, schools in session, hospitals.
  • Today the incident's planning staff put that picture together by hand.
  • This server automates that work, not the physics.

Sources: docs/incidents/incident_hotspots_mid_atlantic.svg, docs/incidents/incident_hotspots.md, docs/evidence/hb219/plain_words.md, DN-001

Slide 5 of 22, Problem statement: Today's tools draw the area, not who is inside it. - That fusion is done today by a Situation Unit by hand. (DN-001) - The reader is an Incident Commander or a Planning Section Chief under time pressure. Solution overview

In: the incident. Out: a brief

  • Given a hazmat accident in transport (material, container, place, time), it gathers public federal data into the area to protect, warnings that each name their source, and a draft Incident Command System briefing form (ICS 201).
  • Every distance comes from the federal Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG).
  • The server runs no dispersion model; the application draws a labelled modelled cloud.
  • No tool result and no ICS 201 carries a modelled value.

Sources: docs/submission/demo/csx_night_first_view.png, deck_screenshots.py (a build tool held privately), docs/evidence/hb219/plain_words.md, DN-001, README.md

Solution overview

The modelled gas cloud, by level of health effect, over time

  • The application draws one modelled cloud for each level of health effect (Acute Exposure Guideline Levels AEGL-3, AEGL-2 and AEGL-1), from the one model a published test chooses for the release.
  • The cloud is drawn for every 15 minutes of its time, each step shown as soon as it is computed, with a Play control.
  • The protective action distance is the guidebook's.

Sources: docs/evidence/hb192/csx_night_frame_180.png, the HB-192 evidence (held privately), docs/evidence/hb219/plain_words.md, README.md

Solution overview

The timeline, as evidence, and the checklist

  • The timeline is evidence, and the list of events for an exercise; it is not the commander's view for decisions.
  • Each row is one place reaching one health-effect level.
  • The checklist exists to remind the reader to think critically about the brief and the quality of its information.
  • A line that later data made false is struck through, not removed.

Solution overview

Other uses, from the author's decisions

  • A quick answer: the material's four-digit number and a place in, first actions out, short enough to read aloud.
  • A drill generator: practice scenarios placed along a named rail line or road.
  • The list of events for an exercise, filled from the timeline: each event's number, time and message.
  • a worst-case scenario builder, perhaps a top-five list for exercises and planning.
  • Who is there by day: workers as well as residents.

Technical approach and key decisions

Seven tools, each a question a commander asks

ToolWhat it reads
assess_incidentbundled reference data; sunrise and sunset by the federal solar equations
protective_action_footprintbundled reference data; the National Weather Service forecast when no wind is given
population_at_riskCensus Bureau maps and population counts; a cached file of where people work
facilities_in_footprintfederal maps of buildings, water and transport; a cached file of hospitals and nursing homes
receiving_hospitalsthe cached file of hospitals and nursing homes only
material_response_guidancebundled reference data only
build_ics_201the six tools above; Census Bureau places, counties and roads; National Weather Service points
  • The hazbrief brief application is a client of the server, not part of it.

Sources: docs/evidence/hb219/plain_words.md, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, README.md

Built ahead of time, served at run time

  end

    APP["app.py<br/>FastMCP, stdio or HTTP"] --> TOOLS["tools/ (7)<br/>prompts/ (2), resources/ (3)"]
    TOOLS --> LOAD["packs.py<br/>verify at startup"]
    TOOLS --> FLAGS["flags.py<br/>deterministic evaluator"]

  LODES --> TOOLS

  HTTP --> CEN["api.census.gov<br/>tigerweb.geo.census.gov"]

  • It reads six checked data files, two cached file sets and six live federal services. It writes nothing back and calls no model.
  • No database is opened at runtime

Technical approach and key decisions

One model per release, and a source on every number

  • A published test (the critical Richardson number) classes the release as a dense gas, a gas that drifts with the air, or not classed.
  • A dense gas is modelled by SCICHEM, a dispersion model from the Electric Power Research Institute, on the forecast wind, hour by hour.
  • A release the test cannot class is not modelled, and the brief says why.
  • Every number carries its source: the tool output it came from, with its value, or a document and page.
  • Point of Rocks night scenario, first picture of the cloud; the page's size before and after a fix: 14.2 seconds; 6.62 megabytes, then 3.39 megabytes

Sources: docs/evidence/hb219/plain_words.md, README.md, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/submission/EVALUATION.md

Technical approach and key decisions

Three decisions the evaluation forced

  • Reading the tables as data found the ERG's own errors.
  • A rule the language model is expected to follow is a hope. A rule the server applies, with its reason in the output, is a guarantee, and the model only narrates it.
  • A tool result that is correct but over the model's size limit never reaches the model.

Sources: docs/submission/EVALUATION.md, docs/evidence/hb219/plain_words.md

Technical approach and key decisions

How it is tested: four levels, two steps

  • Every collected test runs in exactly one of the two steps, and both must pass.
LevelWhat it tests
Part A: fixed rules on every outputEvery output the tools can produce obeys the server's fixed rules.
Part B: saved scenarios rerunNo change moves any tool output on any saved scenario unnoticed.
Part C: live sourcesWhether the federal sources the server reads still answer as they did when the test scenarios were recorded.
Part D: the language model's repliesIs every number and name in its reply backed by a tool output?

Sources: docs/submission/EVALUATION.md, docs/evidence/hb219/plain_words.md

Technical approach and key decisions

Backup: each model, where it is appropriate, and its limits

  • MG: the geometric mean of measured over predicted concentration; 1 means no difference.
ModelProvidesAppropriate forStable trialsLimits
SCICHEMthe levels, their times and the cloud on the forecast wind hour by houra dense release under classes A to D, at every wind speedobserved over predicted MG 3.50 (95 percent 2.87 to 4.27)Not established under classes E and F
SLABevery level's extent checkwhere any hour of the horizon is class E or FMG 0.87 (95 percent 0.76 to 1.00)it gives no times and does not turn with the forecast
